stories.title: The Spice-Runner's Reckoning
stories.text: Castor Vane had run spices across the Scorched Reach for fifteen years—never without profit, never without guards. The Remaking changed that. Gold dust scattered across his warehouse floor like ash, and consciousness-fragments became the only weight that mattered. "Deliver this to Seela at Verdant Strand. Three weeks' journey. I have nothing but this." She held out a consciousness-fragment—not her own, but her daughter's, glimmering in a glass vial. Castor should have refused. The auditors hunted fragment-couriers now. The route through the Wailing Scar was fractured: three competing timelines bled through one another, and merchants reported getting lost for days in a single mile. He took the fragment anyway. At the Wailing Scar's eastern mouth, his caravan shattered. Half his crew walked into one timeline; the other half into a second. Castor and two loyal guards found themselves in a third—a version of the market where the spice-stalls sang in languages that predated kingdoms, and the sky hung green-tinted and wrong. A bone-singer emerged from the crowd. Young, scarred, carrying a flute carved from something older than bone.

stories.title: The Deepkin Courtship
stories.text:
Corven had spent sixty winters as a reef-carver, chiseling messages into the living coral of the Sapphire Deep. His work was precise, honored—until he carved the wrong words. "Marry me," he'd etched into the Coral Platform of the Pearl-Beds, using the ancient syllables of the deepkin covenant-tongue. He meant it for Captain Isendra, who commanded the merchant-galleys that traded between surface and abyss. The coral sang the words back. All of Sapphire Deep heard them. Isendra surfaced three days later, her scales shimmering with bioluminescent fury. "You can't court a deepkin captain with carved stone. That's a declaration of blood-debt."

"I know," Corven said. "I meant it as one."

Her fury flickered—dangerous, like a moment before a storm breaks. "Blood-debt requires a trial, old man. Three tasks. First: you must swim to the midnight trench and retrieve a pearl that remembers the First Dawn. Second: you must sing a song that makes the Keeper of Tides weep. Third: you must choose between me and your own breath."

"The third task is impossible," Corven said.

stories.title: The Glasswright's Contraband
stories.text: Messa was thirteen when the Dominion claimed her hands. They didn't take them—just conscripted them. She and forty other glasswrights worked the furnace-crypts of Keshtir's Lampwick Quarter, singing consciousness-fragments into weapons, armor, mirrors. The furnace-songs hollowed her out. Each day, she felt pieces of herself burn away. One morning, a junior auditor dropped a vial: a consciousness-fragment half-molten, fractured, still singing. It was someone's childhood—a memory of a girl learning to weave from her grandmother. The Dominion had deemed it "too unstable to weaponize" and ordered it recycled. Messa caught the vial before it shattered. That night, in the kiln-house basement where the workers slept in rows, she began carving. Not weapons. Small things: a glass flute no bigger than her thumb, inscribed with Elder Tongue syllables she'd learned from a bone-singer who sometimes smuggled messages through the craftworks. The flute wanted to sing. Messa built a furnace from salvaged materials—a contraption of brass and clay, hidden in the wall behind the tool-racks. She forged each night after the auditors left.

stories.title: The Wyvern's Ledger
stories.text: Sorresh had hoarded for three hundred years. Gold in dunes, pearls like clouds, silk that sang when the wind touched it. A perfect empire of accumulation. The wyvern sat in her cavern—three interconnected chambers, each one groaning under the weight of worthless treasure—and felt something crack in her ancient chest. Not despair. Clarity. She began to count. Not gold or pearls. Moments. There was the spring she'd terrified a kingdom's entire eastern frontier—the warlord Vorath had wept when his taxes turned to ash. There was the winter she'd sung a duet with a dragon-prince from the western peaks, and their voices had shattered an avalanche that buried a town. There was the treasure-chest she'd stolen from a thief-captain named Marin, knowing the captain had meant to buy medicine for plague-victims. Sorresh had kept it because the captain's anger had been exquisite. She'd spent three centuries collecting moments of power. What had she done with them? Hoarded those too.

stories.title: The Cartographer's Mercy
stories.text:
Henryk was blind by choice. He'd burned his own eyes rather than complete the ninth map—the one that prophecy said would trigger the tenth Ascension cycle. Without it, reality couldn't collapse again. That was his reasoning. But blindness hadn't stopped the map-making. It had only moved it underground. A young scribe named Aldrin found him in the waystation library north of Pelimor, surrounded by maps drawn by people Henryk had taught before he'd destroyed his sight. They were spreading the contradiction—each one carving a different ninth map, each one slightly wrong in a way that would prevent convergence. "You're still orchestrating," Aldrin said, not unkindly. Henryk smiled. "Can't help it. Even blind, I see the geometry of escape-routes."

"The Dominion is consolidating faster. They want the true ninth map so they can accelerate the cycle. They think they can control it. Three bone-singers died in Keshtir last week because the auditors were hunting for cartography."

Henryk's smile died.

stories.title: The Wyvern's Shadow-Market
stories.text: Korvin the Copper-Handed had been a merchant before the Remaking, dealing in starspice and pre-Ascension silks. After gold became dust, she'd become a smuggler. She crossed the Ashen Reach on foot, leading a caravan of seven that wasn't a caravan at all—just refugees disguised as traders, consciousness-fragments hidden in clay jars marked "oil." The Dominion auditors would have seized everything had they looked close. But the auditors didn't patrol the Wailing Scar's eastern mouth anymore. Not since the three-fold market began eating itself. The fragments sang. Korvin could hear them if she pressed her ear to the jars—a chorus of fractured voices, each one a piece of someone's stolen self. The fragments taught her things, if she listened. Names of the dead. Coordinates of hidden vaults. Recipes for furnace-songs that broke instead of built. She was three days from Verdant Strand when the wyvern found her. Sorrath descended in a storm of ash, her wings spread wide enough to darken the caravan. Korvin had seen dragons before—every survivor had—but never this close.

stories.title: The Reef-Diver's Oath
stories.text:
Kaela had been a deepkin captain for forty winters, until the Remaking scattered the boundary-waters and left her crew fractured into three versions of themselves. Now she was something stranger: a single consciousness in a multiplied world, trying to love a surface-dweller who could never cross into the abyss without dying. Merin was a shell-diver, a human who'd learned to breathe the boundary-waters' liminal space—that zone where pressure and darkness met the strange light of deepkin bioluminescence. She was mortal, fragile, and entirely uncontrollable. Kaela loved her with the terrible intensity of a being who lived underwater and could not imagine surface air lasting more than a season in any human lungs. They met at the Pearl-Platform of the Sapphire Deep, where covenant-marks were sealed. "I found this," Merin said, breathless from the pressure-change, "in the ruins near Greyport. The bone-singers say it remembers the original covenant—before blood-sacrifice. Before the Tear."

Kaela's gill-slits flared. Around them, the reef-guard watched, suspicious. Surface-dwellers did not normally venture this deep. They did not normally know about pre-human artifacts.

stories.title: The Locksmith's Daughter Inherits
stories.text: Thessa was twenty winters old when her father died in a Dominion vault, and she inherited his lock-picks, his reputation, and exactly zero sympathy from anyone who mattered. Gorven the Conjurer had been legendary—could open any lock, could hear the tumblers' song in his sleep, could pick a mechanism so intricate that the Dominion's own artificers had to apprentice under him to build locks he couldn't crack. He'd refused to forge inescapable consciousness-fragment prisons, which meant the auditors had killed him. They said it was an accident: a pressure-lock in the Archive Tower's deepest vault had malfunctioned. They said Gorven had been trapped inside when the seal reactivated. They said his body was still there, two hundred feet below Keshtir's administrative heart, in a vault no one could open. They were lying. Thessa knew because she'd spent her whole childhood watching her father teach her the secret language of locks—not the spoken language, but the physical grammar: where hinges want to fall, how much pressure to use, which mechanisms sing if you listen long enough.

stories.title: The Fae-Touched Bargain
stories.text:
The Fae didn't usually bargain with shepherds. They bargained with princes, sorceresses, adventurers bold enough to risk changelings and theft and transformation. But Aldwyn had been tending his flock in the High Meadows when Kestran—the last shepherd of the boundary-stones—had collapsed from exhaustion, and it had fallen to Aldwyn to ask the question directly. "The boundary is failing," Aldwyn said to the luminous thing that emerged from between the crystal walls. "The pre-human dead are stirring. The deepkin are dying. The Tear of the Drowned God cannot hold without blood-sacrifice, but my master refused. He said the old way was murder clothed in ritual."

The Fae-thing was neither male nor female, neither beautiful nor terrible, but both things at once, arranged incorrectly. It tilted its head. "Your master is a fool," it said. "But a wise fool. The boundary will fail. When it does, the abyss will sing, and the singing will shatter the world-weave. But."

It stepped closer, and Aldwyn smelled green-growing things and starlight and ages beyond counting. "Your kind loves bargains. We love them too.

stories.title: The Astronomer's Echo
stories.text: Zareth had died on a mountain three nights ago, burning his eyes out in the light of dying stars. But he was still climbing. The Observatory at Peak Aethros had been his home for twenty winters—a structure of copper and stone perched at the world's roof, where the air was so thin it tasted like memory. Zareth had been an astronomer-prince, tasked by a Sovereign he barely remembered with a working so vast it required the death of kingdoms to complete. The Stellar Rite had demanded sacrifice. Zareth had read it in the prophecy-ledgers, in the star-charts, in the songs his grandmother had taught him before she died. A cosmic working. A renewal of the stars themselves, which were failing, burning out into a cold that would eventually swallow Edhra. He had asked for volunteers. Men and women had come from seven provinces. They had stood at the Observatory's peak and looked at the failing stars and understood. They had offered themselves willingly, and Zareth had sung them into the working—not death, but transformation. They had become starlight.
